title: Our Seasons Tree
strapline: One tree, visited all year — bare, then blossoming, then green, then gold — the turning year written in branches.
intent: Adopting a single tree and visiting it across the whole year gives children a slow, unforgettable story of the seasons, told by something they know and love.
Noticing what has changed since last time grows careful observation, memory and the language of comparison — before and after, then and now.
Children build genuine knowledge of the seasonal cycle and of how living things respond to it — bare in winter, budding in spring, full in summer, shedding in autumn.
Photographing, drawing and recording the same tree over months lays early foundations of gathering data and seeing patterns over time.
Returning to the same familiar spot builds a sense of belonging, of a place that is 'ours', and of caring about the natural world close to home.
The year's language grows with the tree — bud, blossom, leaf, shade, bare, branch, season, change.
implementation: Choose one tree children can reach easily and visit it at the turn of each season — and often in between — with a camera, paper and magnifiers.
Each visit, look closely and compare: 'What's different since we came last time? What's happening to the leaves now?'
Keep a growing record — a photo, a rubbing, a drawing, a collected leaf — displayed in order so the year's story is visible.
Model the wondering: 'Why do you think the tree is bare now? What do you think we'll see next time we come?'
Bring in maths and sequencing — order the photos through the year, count the buds, compare how full the tree is now against a month ago.
Link it to the whole outdoors — what else is changing when the tree changes, what the weather is doing, what the birds and minibeasts are up to.
key_questions: What's different since we came last time?
Why do you think the tree is bare now?
What do you think we'll see next time we come?
How full is the tree now, compared with a month ago?
How many buds can you count on this branch?
